items.followUp: What is the difference between a bonding pair and a non-bonding pair of electrons?

rubric.why: Checks that a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a lone pair is an electron pair on an atom that is not shared with another atom.

rubric.why: Checks that a bond pair is shared between atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a bond pair is an electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons on an atom that is not shared with another atom.
A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.

items.followUp: Define diffusion and give one example of it.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of diffusion as the spreading or mixing of particles.
rubric.how: Award for describing the spontaneous movement or mixing of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration.

rubric.why: Distinguishes effusion from general mixing of particles.
rubric.how: Award for describing the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole, usually into a vacuum or a region of lower pressure.

modelAnswer: Diffusion is the spontaneous mixing of particles due to their random motion, from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration.
Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum or a region of lower pressure.

items.followUp: What is the difference between a saturated solution and an unsaturated solution?

rubric.why: Checks the defining solute limit of a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.

rubric.why: Checks that an unsaturated solution can still dissolve additional solute.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it contains less than the maximum amount of solute and can dissolve more at that temperature.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.

items.followUp: Why do the particles of a suspension settle on standing?

rubric.why: Checks that suspension particles are not uniformly mixed at the particle level.
rubric.how: Award for stating that suspension particles are unevenly distributed, so the mixture is heterogeneous rather than homogeneous.

rubric.why: Checks the reason the suspension lacks uniform composition.
rubric.description: Explains why it is not homogeneous.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that its particles remain separate rather than dissolving and may settle on standing.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture because its particles are not uniformly distributed throughout the mixture.
The suspended particles do not dissolve and remain separate; they may settle on standing.

items.followUp: State the rule “like dissolves like” and give an example involving a non-polar solvent.

rubric.why: Checks the principle that solute and solvent with similar polarity tend to dissolve one another.
rubric.how: Award for stating that polar substances dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents.

rubric.why: Checks that the rule is supported by a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award for a correct example, such as water dissolving salt or sugar, or benzene dissolving grease.

modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that substances with similar nature or polarity dissolve in one another: polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents.
For example, polar salt dissolves in polar water.

items.followUp: Write five properties of canal rays.

rubric.why: Checks the origin and direction or path of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award for stating that cathode rays originate at the cathode and travel towards the anode, in straight lines.

rubric.why: Checks the charge carried by cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award for identifying cathode rays as negatively charged.

rubric.why: Checks their response to an electric field, consistent with negative charge.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.

rubric.why: Checks a visible effect produced when cathode rays strike certain materials.
rubric.how: Award for stating that cathode rays produce fluorescence or a glow on suitable materials.

rubric.why: Checks that their nature does not depend on the gas or electrode material used.
rubric.description: States their independence from the source materials.
rubric.how: Award for stating that cathode rays have the same properties regardless of the gas in the tube or the material of the electrodes.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays originate from the cathode and travel towards the anode in straight lines.
They carry a negative charge.
They are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain materials.
Their properties are independent of the gas in the discharge tube and the material of the electrodes.

items.followUp: Explain why ice has a lower density than liquid water.

rubric.why: Checks recognition of the intermolecular attraction involved.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules involving hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.

rubric.why: Checks the atoms commonly involved in hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award for identifying hydrogen attached to F, O or N and attraction to a lone pair on F, O or N.

rubric.why: Checks the characteristic structure formed by hydrogen bonds in ice.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open, cage-like or hexagonal arrangement in ice.

rubric.why: Checks how the ice structure affects molecular spacing.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the open arrangement keeps water molecules farther apart than in liquid water.

rubric.why: Checks the link between greater spacing and floating.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ice is less dense than liquid water and therefore floats.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on an electronegative atom of another molecule.
In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open, cage-like hexagonal structure.
This structure keeps the molecules farther apart than they are in liquid water.
Consequently, ice has a lower density than liquid water.
An object less dense than the liquid floats, so ice floats in water.

rubric.why: Checks that physical chemistry applies physical principles to chemical systems or processes.
rubric.how: Award for describing physical chemistry as the branch that applies physical principles to chemical substances, systems or processes.

rubric.why: Checks that biochemistry deals with chemical processes or substances in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award for describing biochemistry as the study of chemical substances and reactions in living organisms.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry applies the principles of physics to chemical substances and processes.
Biochemistry is the study of chemical substances and reactions that occur in living organisms.
